He also emphasized asking the right question at the right time and using whatever means will answer it.

sections.heading: The mistake
sections.content: In the HipChat effort, the team believed it could win the market while also handling a rewrite and platformization; Crusson later said doing all of that at once was too much. More broadly, he recognized that approaches and assumptions behind Atlassian’s past success might not work for a new product, and that the team had not talked enough to a different set of users.

sections.heading: What he learned to do instead
sections.content: Validate key hypotheses much earlier, before it is too late or before writing code. For Jira Product Discovery, the team tested demand with an ad in a Jira newsletter and a landing page inviting product managers to join a waitlist; it got more than 3,000 signups in two weeks. His approach was to establish that there was a problem and market, explore whether proposed solutions addressed customers’ problems, and prioritize learning with customers. If the platform was not ready, he said to hack and iterate with customers first, then platformize what proved useful.

answer.summary: Crusson said he had relied too much on assumptions drawn from Atlassian’s past success and planned to build first, then distribute. He learned to test key assumptions early—before writing code—using lightweight customer-facing experiments.

sections.heading: The mistake
sections.content: He assumed that because product managers were already using Jira, Atlassian could build a product for them and distribute it through Jira. More broadly, he learned that the assumptions behind Atlassian’s previous success would not necessarily work for a new product.
